question: Where shared-GPU self-play game processes spend CPU per game: search, rules and input preparation.

run.malloc_nano_zone: 0 (inherited from the agent session environment; the tiny allocator was used)
run.games_per_hour_note: Not comparable with the 24.2 games/h run (b89e86d). Game CPU per evaluation was 7% higher (14.60 vs 13.62 ms); instrumentation explains at least a fifth of that and the rules commits since b89e86d were not measured separately. The coordinator sets the pace, and its model calls took 14% longer (7.67 vs 6.75 ms) on slightly smaller batches (3.98 vs 4.12 positions), which accounts for the 16% lower evaluation rate (478 vs 566 per second with every slot playing). Why they were slower was not measured; other applications were running on the machine.
run.game_time_note: search includes waiting for evaluations and input preparation

game_wall_split.neither_note: much of it waiting for the interpreter lock (take_gil 13-29% of game-thread samples)

profile.accounting: Each game thread charges time.thread_time_ns to the innermost wrapped call; categories sum exactly to thread CPU.

instrumentation.note: Included in the categories, about half in the wrapped call and half in its caller. A lower bound; clock reads alone cost 11.6 s per game in the run, so 25-35 s is plausible.

native_samples.process: one game process (seeds 1966, 1972, 1973, 1975), 30 s at 600, 2400 and 4000 s
native_samples.busy_definition: Not under take_gil/_PyThreadState_Attach and not ending in a blocking leaf (read, __psynch_cvwait, __psynch_mutexwait, __ulock_wait2, write).
native_samples.caveat: Busy samples were about twice the measured CPU rate (21-27% of wall time), so samples give the make-up of busy CPU, not CPU seconds. Work tied to game phases varies between windows.

search_logic_92_5_s.engine_clone_destruction: 35-42 s (two thirds freeing the leaf's cached observation JSON)
search_logic_92_5_s.tree_code: 17-42 s (about 30 s; score_actions is the largest part)

allocator_ab.workload: whole random 11-round games through the adapter and rules engine, one thread, verify-input-prep/rgame.py, alternating runs, load average about 7 from other applications
allocator_ab.untested: the effect with 4 threads per process, 8 processes and the coordinator

candidates.basis: CPU-seconds per game out of 1,250, from in-run costs and native-sample shares; each estimate was checked by an independent verifier who re-derived it from the raw data and reran the scripts.

keep_moves_dice_and_search_results.change: validate only history events added by the transition
keep_moves_dice_and_search_results.risk: very low; keep the full check on restore, construction, serialization and tests

keep_moves_dice_and_search_results.change: assemble each evaluation's menu arrays in one native call
build the observation JSON with moves instead of copies
apply moves in place on throwaway search copies
keep_moves_dice_and_search_results.risk: a copy that fails mid-move must refuse all later calls; other engines share cloneForSearch

keep_moves_dice_and_search_results.change: hardware SHA-256 for the planning key
keep_moves_dice_and_search_results.risk: low; byte-identical keys, 5.8 times faster in a scratch benchmark

keep_moves_dice_and_search_results.change: let Engine::step's legality check validate tree moves instead of rebuilding the menu
keep_moves_dice_and_search_results.risk: low; identical stub searches in 60 of 60 positions, same outcomes in 2,781 stale/foreign cases

keep_moves_dice_and_search_results.change: cheaper graph compile: lock-free caches, one probe per string, native numeric features
keep_moves_dice_and_search_results.risk: native features must match Python bit for bit

keep_moves_dice_and_search_results.change: smaller items: position text, action snapshots, numeric_input, edge scoring, small caches
skip the economy re-check after the engine's own legality check
keep_moves_dice_and_search_results.risk: medium; only for actions Engine::step has just matched; relies on a cross-module guarantee verified for the current code; keep the check for actions the rules build themselves, such as the approved rail purchase (src/economy.cpp:703-704)

keep_moves_dice_and_search_results.change: reuse the previous search's network evaluations (keyed by model version and planning key)
keep_moves_dice_and_search_results.risk: same priors and values; clear on weight updates; also removes 25-30% of coordinator work by count; duplicate rate measured with stand-in evaluators
keep_moves_dice_and_search_results.overlap_with_one_move_skip: repeats are 48-52% of evaluations in one-move searches against 20-25% elsewhere; after the skip, reuse saves at most about 65-80 s and the two together cut at most about 35-40% of evaluations, not 44-49%

decisions_for_the_user.change: play the only legal move without a search
decisions_for_the_user.effect: moves, dice and training samples unchanged provided the skip still draws the decision's search seed and move-sampling random number; 18.6% fewer evaluations; search traces lose statistics for those moves; a bit-for-bit check needs a deterministic evaluator

decisions_for_the_user.change: skip the rest of the structural check on search copies only
decisions_for_the_user.effect: on top of the incremental history check (about 130-150 s instead of it); removes the rules-bug tripwire on 99.4% of transitions

decisions_for_the_user.change: search passes through one-move positions without evaluating them (algorithm change)
decisions_for_the_user.effect: moves about 18% of evaluations to positions with a choice; needs an equal-compute strength test

configuration.change: use the default macOS allocator for game processes

candidates.combined: The first nine changes sum to 486-636 s, about 40-50% of game-process CPU. The one-move skip then removes about a fifth of what remains (about 130-160 s), about 50-60% in all; its 255-260 s today does not add to the nine. Contention changes per-call costs 1.5-3.6 times, so the whole must be re-measured in the 8x4 configuration.

limits: One instrumented run; native samples of one process in three 30 s windows.
Single-thread micro-benchmarks run 1.5-3.6 times faster per call than the loaded run for substantial calls, and far faster for tiny ones.
Other applications kept the machine's load average near 7 during the analysis.

CPU savings alone raise games per hour little at the same concurrency, because the coordinator spent 88% of the run in model calls and waited for requests only 2% of it; larger gains need more concurrent games or fewer evaluations.
No learning updates; nothing here measures playing strength.
